articles_used.title: UK and EU to agree youth mobility scheme, BBC understands
articles_used.summary_raw: The scheme is expected to be approved at Friday's UK-EU summit, with new deals on food trade and carbon emissions also on the table.
articles_used.full_text:
This video can not be played
Watch: Burnham says he wants 'best deal for Britain' at UK-EU summit
Up to 100,000 young people from the EU would be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK per year under a new youth mobility scheme set to be agreed on Friday, the BBC understands.
The same number of young Britons would be allowed into Europe under the scheme, expected to be approved at the UK-EU summit in Brussels. Downing Street has not commented on the details, but said talks were "down to the wire" on Thursday.
The prime minister has said a "Channel action plan" on immigration could also be struck, while negotiators are seeking agreements on food trade rules and carbon emissions pricing.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of "reopening the divisions" of the Brexit referendum.
A new youth mobility scheme would aim to make it easier for young people to work and travel both in the EU and UK.
The UK already has schemes in place with 13 non-EU countries including Australia, Canada and India.
In 2024, the EU proposed allowing 18 to 30 year-olds to work or study in the EU and UK for up to four years.
Labour, which was then in opposition, rejected the deal - arguing it amounted to reinstating freedom of movement.
Since coming to government, the party has suggested it would consider a more restricted scheme with a time limit, a cap on the numbers coming to the UK and a ban on participants from claiming benefits.
The UK's request to limit numbers has proved to be a sticking point in negotiation ahead of the summit, along with the EU's request that EU students should pay the same tuition fees at UK universities as domestic students.
Speaking to broadcasters on Thursday evening, Burnham was asked if there were any circumstances in which the UK would walk away from a deal on Friday.
"There would always be those circumstances because I'm in this to get the best deal for Britain, always," he said.
"But what's in it for us is the possibility of lower food prices and I can't turn my back on that, lower costs for business, cutting red tape, and a really big win potentially of more collaboration on immigration - a Channel action plan - which is a really big deal if we can land that tomorrow.
"So I hope people can understand why I have pushed this because it could be a really good deal for Britain."
Burnham previously said the UK and EU could link up their law enforcement efforts, including sharing more data and criminal records of foreign nationals.
The prime minister's spokesman has said if a deal were secured, the government would introduce legislation to Parliament next week to implement changes.
The Brexit debate is back – and there are nerves about what happens next
Faisal Islam: What's in the Brexit reset food deal and are there trade-offs?
The EU that Burnham is eyeing up is very different to the one Britain left
An agreement on trade could remove checks and paperwork faced by food companies exporting to the EU.
The government argues this could add £5bn to the economy and cut food prices.
However, it could mean the UK will have to follow certain EU rules on products, for example on gene-edited crops or labelling.
Burnham has also said the summit would allow the UK to raise concernsabout the Made in Europe scheme,which is designed to protect industries from unfair Chinese competition.
Burnham has previously suggested he could commit Labour to building a closer long-term future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member - however, he has ruled out major changes before the next election.
The party's 2024 manifesto promised not to return to the EU, the single market, customs union or freedom of movement, which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa.
Earlier this week, former deputy prime minister David Lammy urged the prime minister to go into the next general election promising to rejoin the EU.
However, the subjecthas divided his cabinetwith one minister warning of the costs that would come with reversing Brexit.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage,speaking to The Sun,external, said he does "not believe for a minute" the country would "ever vote to rejoin" the EU.
He added: "I think what Burnham is doing is playing a very cynical political game. He's trying to pick up votes from the Lib Dems, pick up votes from the Greens, and using it as a massive distraction from all the problems that he can't deal with."
Speaking to the BBC's Today programme on Thursday, Badenoch said she wanted to see easier trading with the EU, but "not trade at any cost".
She also said the new deals could see UK companies having to follow EU rules, even those that do not trade with the bloc.
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey told BBC Newsnight that while he agreed with Burnham on "the harms of Brexit", he did not think the prime minister was "going to go anywhere near far enough".
"We need to go further and faster," he said, including returning to freedom of movement - which Sir Ed said would help tackle immigration and boost the UK economy.

articles_used.title: Pistorius will Militärpakt mit Polen ausbauen
articles_used.summary_raw: Patriot-Systeme und Eurofighter-Kampfjets sowie eine Zusammenarbeit der Armeen beim Aufbau von gemeinsamen Verteidigungsstellungen: Polen und Deutschland arbeiten bereits militärisch zusammen. Das möchten beide Länder nun intensivieren.
articles_used.full_text:
Inhalte zeigen von:
Externe Anbieter:
Stand: 20.11.2026 • 04:53 Uhr
Patriot-Systeme und Eurofighter-Kampfjets sowie eine Zusammenarbeit der Armeen beim Aufbau von gemeinsamen Verteidigungsstellungen: Polen und Deutschland arbeiten bereits militärisch zusammen. Das möchten beide Länder nun intensivieren.
Deutschland und Polen wollen ihrim Sommer geschlossenes Verteidigungsabkommenbis zu den Regierungskonsultationen im Januar mit Leben füllen.
Ein entsprechender Fahrplan solle bis zu dem Treffen in Warschau ausgearbeitet werden, um die nächsten Schritte zur Umsetzung des Pakts einzuleiten, sagte Bundesverteidigungsminister Boris Pistorius nach einem Gespräch mit seinem polnischen Amtskollegen Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz in der polnischen Hauptstadt.
Damit werde die enge Zusammenarbeit zwischen den Streitkräften gestärkt und gemeinsam Verantwortung für Europa übernommen, erklärte Pistorius.
Analyse19.11.2026
Mit Erinnerungskultur will Verteidigungsminister Pistorius im Nachbarland für eine starke Partnerschaft werben.mehr
Kosiniak-Kamysz betonte, beide Seiten wollten vor allem die Kooperation in der Rüstungsindustrie ausbauen. Gemeinsame Initiativen der Unternehmen sollten Europa unabhängiger von anderen Kontinenten machen, Lieferketten sichern und eine ausreichende Waffenproduktion gewährleisten.
Beide Länder hatten das Abkommen im Juni unterzeichnet, um der Bedrohung durch Russland zu begegnen. Pistorius verwies in Warschau auf die laufende militärische Zusammenarbeit zum Schutz der NATO-Ostflanke. Die Bundeswehr verlege bei dem Manöver "Grand Eagle" derzeit mehr als 2.000 Soldaten sowie rund 50 Ketten- und 650 Radfahrzeuge durch Polen.
Deutschland unterstütze das Nachbarland zudem mit Patriot-Systemen und Eurofighter-Kampfjets bei der Luftverteidigung, während Pioniere beider Staaten seit dem Sommer gemeinsam Verteidigungsstellungen aufbauten.

articles_used.title: China issues Mount Fuji warning as family of missing climber offers reward
articles_used.summary_raw: The $75,000 reward offered by Chen Jie's family has sparked fears of more reckless climbing attempts.
articles_used.full_text:
The $75,000 reward offered by Chen Jie's family has sparked fears of more reckless climbing attempts
The Chinese embassy in Japan has warned its citizens against off-season ascents of Mount Fuji amid concerns that the hefty reward offered by a missing hiker's family could encourage more reckless climbing.
Chen Jie, 25, vanished on 8 November on the mountain. His family is offering 500,000 yuan ($75,000; £57,300) to anyone who finds him alive, and 100,000 yuan to anyone who recovers his body, say Chinese and Japanese media reports.
Strong winds and blizzards pose serious risks during the closed season, especially as shelter and first-aid centres are not operational, the embassy said on Tuesday.
Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from around early July to early September.
Earlier this year, authorities of Yamanashi province, where the northern part of Mount Fuji sits, had said that people who attempt to climb Mount Fuji during off-peak seasons and then require rescue by helicopter will have topay for the servicefrom next year on.
Authorities will also require those looking to scale Fuji during the off-season to submit detailed climbing plans.
"We hope that these measures will cause people to rethink what climbing Mount Fuji during the winter is like," Kotaro Nagasaki, the prefecture governor, said at the time.
On Wednesday, Nagasaki told reporters that attempts to find the missing climber could lead to "secondary disasters"
According to Japanese news outlet the Mainichi Shimbun, Nagasaki appeared to appeal to Chen's family, saying: "I understand that your family is important, but please refrain from doing anything that could endanger others."
Some social media users in Japan have similarly expressed fears would entice people to venture into the mountains ill-prepared and lead to more accidents,
Yamanashi police said Chen had set out on his hike on 8 November with two friends, who turned back after they realised the mountain was closed and that they weren't suitably equipped for the conditions of the trails.
Chen pressed on alone from the fifth station of the Yoshida Trail, which sits at around 2,300m (7545ft) above sea level.
A friend last heard from Chen at 10:30 that day, when he sent a video message saying: "I'm going up the mountain... There's no one in sight."
The highest point of Mount Fuji, which is Japan's tallest peak, stands at 3,776m.
Local authorities launched a search for Chen on 10 November, but it had to be halted several times because of poor weather.
Chen's father reportedly arrived in Japan on 13 November. It is not clear when he posted the reward offer.

articles_used.title: In Dutzenden Städten: Jugendproteste in ganz Deutschland
articles_used.summary_raw: In Dutzenden Städten sind Proteste angekündigt. Unter anderem die Bundesschülerkonferenz, "Schulstreik gegen die Wehrpflicht", "Gen Z regelt" und Fridays For Future haben heute bundesweit zu Demonstrationen aufgerufen.
articles_used.full_text:
Inhalte zeigen von:
Externe Anbieter:
Stand: 20.11.2026 • 04:16 Uhr
In Dutzenden Städten sind Proteste angekündigt. Unter anderem die Bundesschülerkonferenz, "Schulstreik gegen die Wehrpflicht", "Gen Z regelt" und Fridays For Future haben bundesweit zu Demonstrationen aufgerufen.
Heute mobilisieren bundes- und europaweit verschiedene Gruppen zum gemeinsamen Jugendprotest. Mit der Initiative "Gen Z regelt" ruft dabei in Deutschland ein dezentral organisiertes Netzwerk ebenso zur Teilnahme auf wie die Schüler-Gruppe "Schulstreik gegen Wehrpflicht", die bereits mehrfach bundesweit demonstriert hatte. Zur Generation Z zählen, grob gesagt, die von 1995 bis 2010 Geborenen. Auch die Bundesschülerkonferenz plant in Berlin eine Demonstration.
Nicht alle Anliegen werden von den Demonstrierenden geteilt, oft haben sie unterschiedliche Ziele. Auf der Webseite von "Gen Z regelt" werden sechs zentrale Forderungen genannt: Sie treten ein für bessere Bildung, gegen steigende Lebenshaltungskosten und eine ungerechte Lastenverteilung.
Zudem sprechen sie sich gegen Überwachung, für mehr Klimaschutz und gegen die Wehrpflicht aus. Beim letzten Punkt gibt es eine Schnittmenge zu den streikenden Schülerinnen und Schülern, die sich unter dem Motto "Fight for our Future - not their wars" gegen Wehrpflicht und Musterung aussprechen.
18.11.2026
Kürzlich hatte es Rufe nach Verboten von "GenZ"-Demos gegeben. Nun äußern Politiker Verständnis für die Jugendproteste.mehr
Bundesbildungsministerin Karin Prien (CDU) verspricht auf berechtigte Interessen einzugehen. Sie möchte junge Menschen in "politische Entscheidungen einbeziehen". Und: "Unsere dringendste Aufgabe ist Generationengerechtigkeit und dabei muss Bildung Priorität haben." Für Bildung investierten Bund und Länder aber auch bereits erheblich.
Bei den von "Gen Z regelt" organisiertenProtesten am 31. Oktoberwaren bundesweit Zehntausende weitgehend friedlich auf die Straße gegangen. Danach gab es abends in mehreren Städten vereinzelt Ausschreitungen, etwa inFrankfurt am Main. Damals hatte "Gen Z regelt" nach eigenen Angaben mehr als 180.000 Anmeldungen bundesweit.
Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz (CDU), der bei den Demonstrationen aktiv kritisiert wurde, ließ damals über seinen Sprecher mitteilen, dass junge Menschen "legitime Anliegen" verträten, die er "sehr ernst" nehme.

articles_used.title: More climate money for Africa? Europe says use what's already pledged
articles_used.summary_raw: African countries at the UN climate summit in Turkey are demanding more funding from developed nations to help them cope with climate change.
articles_used.full_text:
Northern Uganda is suffering from a severe drought
In Uganda's northern Karamoja region, Elijah Lobur and his family now eat just one meal a day.
A severe drought that began in April has destroyed crops, while food brought in from elsewhere has become increasingly unaffordable.
"Seven months without rain has brought us to this point where we now live in hunger," the 44-year-old farmer, who lives with his grandmother, wife and five children, told the BBC.
"Even some of the wild plants that we used to eat have withered and dried up."
Local officials say more than 90% of crops have failed in the region, where agriculture is largely rain-fed.
Further south, in Malawi, Mathews Nkhambala has experienced the devastating effects of flooding.
In April 2024, barely a year after Tropical Cyclone Freddy devastated the country's southern region, floods displaced people in Chikwawa district.
Nkhambala fled to higher ground with his wife and four children as floodwaters swept through his village.
"As we reached a safe height, we saw our house swept away right in front of our eyes. Everything I had was gone," he told the BBC.
He lost a harvest of 15 bags of sorghum and part of his farmland. His children were so traumatised that they stopped going to school.
"They refused to go to school for many months. They were so disturbed," he recalled.
After relocating and trying to rebuild his life, Nkhambala is now facing another climate challenge - this time a lack of rain.
"This time we fear there may be no harvest. I have no clue what I will do."
A government assessment after Cyclone Freddy found that Malawi had experienced more than 50 disasters linked to storms, floods, landslides and droughts since 1980, affecting millions of people.
While Uganda and Malawi are suffering the effects of climate change and their governments are asking for assistance adapting to the new global weather patterns, they are among 23 African countries yet to submit National Adaptation Plans (NAPs) to the UN climate convention secretariat.
These are the plans that detail how climate change has affected them and the risks they face, and so help make a case for what assistance they need. Without them, experts say, it becomes difficult to secure funding.
"Our region has experienced cyclical droughts for decades, but there has been no action plan to tackle these climate impacts," said Milton Lorpia, who works for Warrior Squad Foundation in Karamoja region of Uganda.
"If only such a plan were in place and implemented, it would certainly have helped us."
Mathews Nkhambala and his wife fear their harvest may fail this year
The African Group of Negotiators at the ongoing UN climate summit (COP31) in Turkey is pushing for adaptation finance to be tripled by 2035, from an annual $40bn (£30bn) baseline that it says developed countries committed to providing by 2025. The interpretation of that commitment remains contested.
The proposal was not accepted for formal negotiations at the summit, although African negotiators have continued to push for it.
The funding is intended to help vulnerable countries prepare for and withstand climate change-induced extreme weather, such as droughts, floods and wildfires.
But the European Union, one of the largest providers of climate finance, says the priority should be ensuring existing commitments reach vulnerable countries rather than setting new funding targets.
"We haven't come to the table with additional monies or additional capital. It's about what we have committed already and ensuring it's deployed," Darragh O'Brien, who leads the EU delegation at COP31 on behalf of the Irish presidency of the Council of the EU, told a press conference.
He acknowledged that developing countries faced difficulties accessing available funding, saying the process needed to be improved.
Wopke Hoekstra, the European Commission's climate commissioner, also argued that the summit should focus on delivering existing pledges rather than making new ones.
"If you are a vulnerable nation in the Pacific or one of the LDCs (Least Developed Countries) and the money is in the bank but does not land on the ground then it is effectively meaningless," he said.
'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted
A really simple guide to climate change
Hoekstra said the EU had provided $30bn of the $100bn in climate finance committed by developed countries in recent years, adding that other wealthy nations should contribute more.
The scale of the need is substantial. According to the UN's Adaptation Gap Report published last year, sub-Saharan Africa requires about $51bn annually in adaptation finance, while the Middle East and North Africa needs $112bn.
Globally, developing countries will need about $300bn annually by 2035, according to the UN's latest report. Yet they received only about 10% of that amount from developed countries in 2024.
Climate-related loss and damage in Africa is projected to cost $440bn between 2020 and 2030, according to Nairobi-based think tank Power Shift Africa.
Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation.
But why have so many African countries failed to prepare plans that could help them identify their needs and build resilience?
"If you look closely, the countries that are yet to submit their NAPs are already dealing with multiple crises, including debt distress, economic pressures and other issues," said David Abudho, climate justice lead at the aid agency, Oxfam.
"Their governments' ability to invest in climate adaptation is limited."
Sheila Apiny, regional climate justice adviser at ActionAid, said the lack of plans reflected a wider shortage of financial and technical support.
"The absence of NAPs in so many countries is, in itself, evidence of an adaptation finance and capacity gap," she argued.
She said this created a vicious cycle - countries lack support to prepare their plans, while not having the plans makes it harder to secure funding for climate resilience.
"When countries lack adequate adaptation planning and, more importantly, the resources to implement those plans, governments are forced into a cycle of responding to disasters instead of preventing or reducing their impacts," said Amos Wemanya, senior climate adviser at Power Shift Africa.
"Instead of investing in early warning systems, climate-resilient agriculture, water security and flood protection, scarce public resources are repeatedly diverted towards emergency relief and reconstruction. This costs more over time and leaves communities increasingly vulnerable."
Under the 2015 Paris climate agreement, developed countries are required to provide financial support to developing nations, including for climate adaptation
African negotiators acknowledge that adaptation plans help countries prioritise investments and attract funding, but argue that their absence should not be used to deny them financial support.
"Of course, having a comprehensive NAP helps countries prioritise investments and prepare proposals for climate finance," said Mahlet Eyassu Melkie, a senior strategic adviser to Ethiopia's COP32 presidency.
"But Africa's adaptation financing needs are based on scientific assessments, climate vulnerability, national priorities and regional estimates – not simply on whether every country has submitted a particular planning document."
The UN Development Programme, which has helped more than 45 countries prepare their plans, said NAPs can help governments mobilise international support and coordinate climate action.
Fred Njehu, a Pan-African political strategist at Greenpeace Africa, said their absence could nevertheless create significant obstacles.
"It is fair to acknowledge that missing adaptation plans act as a major functional barrier that severely bottlenecks the speed, volume and quality of international funding a country can access," he said.
But having a plan does not guarantee the money needed to implement it.
"Even countries that have completed their NAPs have not received money anywhere near what they require for implementation of their adaptation plans," Apiny said.
Kenya offers an example of how adaptation measures can help communities cope with climate pressures.
The walls of the sand dams store water underground when the rivers dry up
In the country's arid and semi-arid south-east, concrete sand dams slow the flow of seasonal rivers, allowing sand to accumulate and store water underground. Communities can access it during dry periods using hand pumps or by scooping it out.
UK charity Sand Dams Worldwide and its local partner, the Africa Sand Dam Foundation, said they had built about 1,300 such dams, improving access to water as droughts become more frequent and intense.
But many vulnerable communities elsewhere on the continent are still waiting for similar interventions.
Back in drought-hit Karamoja, Lobur wonders how different things might have been if farmers had access to small-scale irrigation schemes.
"We do have some underground water sources in some places. If there were proper plans and programmes, we could have tapped them to grow food, but we are having to live in hunger instead," Lobur said.
"My grandmother keeps reminding us how she lost eight children during a famine-like situation in 1982, and we all fear we might perish like that too."

articles_used.title: Medienberichte: Lufthansa will 1.000 Stellen streichen
articles_used.summary_raw: Insgesamt 1.000 Stellen in München und Frankfurt will man bei der Lufthansa Airlines streichen. Das geht aus einem Brief an Mitarbeiter hervor. Auf Anfrage wollte die Airline dem internen Schreiben "nichts hinzufügen".
articles_used.full_text:
Inhalte zeigen von:
Externe Anbieter:
Stand: 20.11.2026 • 02:56 Uhr
Insgesamt 1.000 Stellen in München und Frankfurt will man bei der Lufthansa Airlines streichen. Das geht aus einem Brief an Mitarbeiter hervor. Auf Anfrage wollte die Airline dem internen Schreiben "nichts hinzufügen".
Die Lufthansa-Kernmarke Lufthansa Airlines will einem Medienbericht zufolge an ihren Drehkreuzen Frankfurt und München 1.000 Stellen abbauen. Das geht aus einem Brief von Airline-Chef Jens Ritter und seinen vier Vorstandskollegen an die Belegschaft hervor, derThe Pioneervorlag. "An den Drehkreuzen Frankfurt und München planen wir im Lufthansa Airlines Teilkonzern nun insgesamt 1000 Vollzeitstellen einzusparen", heißt es darin.
Unklar blieb, in welchem Zeitraum und in welcher Form der Stellenabbau erfolgen soll und ob dieser Teil des bereits angekündigten Abbaus ist. Vor gut einem Jahr hatte der Lufthansa-Konzern den Wegfall von rund 4.000 Stellen in der Verwaltung angekündigt. Auf Anfrage wollte das Unternehmen dem internen Schreiben "nichts hinzufügen".
04.11.2026
Hohe Steuern, teure Abgaben: Airlines haben zuletzt viele Flüge an deutschen Flughäfen gestrichen.mehr
Hintergrund sind demnach anhaltende Verluste. Nach neun Monaten liege der operative Verlust bei 180 Millionen Euro. "Durchschnittlich haben wir in den ersten neun Monaten also jeden Monat 20 Millionen Euro Verlust gemacht", erklärte der Vorstand in dem Schreiben.
Das dritte Quartal sei zudem schlechter ausgefallen als das Vorjahresquartal. "Das dritte Jahr in Folge sind wir also finanziell nicht erfolgreich." Lufthansa Airlines sei "bei Kostenstruktur, Effizienz und Produktivität aktuell nicht wettbewerbsfähig". Als Ursachen werden in dem Brief der Krieg in Nahost, hohe Kerosinkosten und neun Streiktage genannt.
In Deutschland arbeiteten Ende 2025 rund 67.100 Menschen bei der Lufthansa Group - rund ein Prozent mehr als im Vorjahr.

articles_used.title: Europe ready for talks with Russia on ending war in Ukraine, leaders say
articles_used.summary_raw: European allies of Ukraine say they have a "united" negotiating position at a summit in Berlin.
articles_used.full_text:
European leaders have said they are ready for negotiations with Russia on ending the war in Ukraine, in a strong show of support for Kyiv.
"Europe has a clear and consistent and united negotiating position," UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz stressed that Moscow's "maximalist demands are not realistic".
They were speaking at Berlin's summit of Ukraine's allies known as the Coalition of the Willing.
Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, one of the two US envoys who were in Berlin, said the US president wanted to make a deal with Moscow "with Europe by his side". Russia's Vladimir Putin has so far rejected any European role in the US-led peace talks.
Trump had earlierheld historic trilateral talks in Shenzhen, south-eastern China, with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping and later dialled into the Berlin summit from Air Force One.
In a lengthy press conference following his talks with Trump and Xi, Putin addressed the question of multilateral peace talks, saying the Americans were "insistently" asking Russia to allow the Europeans to take part.
Putin claimed Russia was not against the idea but said Moscow wanted to clarify "what Europe will bring to these talks".
"That is why, through diplomatic channels, we have invited the Europeans to come to Moscow in order to determine their positions. And after that, we will decide in what format we will continue the dialogue with Ukraine."
But Putin also said that "every day" Russia heard that European leaders were talking about war coming in 2030. "But we are not planning to attack anyone... Is that normal? I do not think so," he said. Still, Putin added, Russia understood that "discussing issues linked to security in Europe is pointless without the Europeans".
Jared Kushner told reporters that the US president had come away from Shenzhen believing that "peace is achievable".
Striking an upbeat note, Kushner said that the Russians were willing to trust the instinct of the US envoys "on our behalf" that the Europeans should be at the table and that Moscow was now "comfortable" with Ukraine having security guarantees based on the idea enshrined in Nato's Article Five that requires allies to come to a country's defence if it comes under attack.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who also was at the summit in Germany's capital, has long sought a guarantee equivalent to Nato's collective defence clause, and there has been little indication that Putin would accept that kind of condition.
Russia rejects outright the idea of Ukrainian membership of Nato, but reports say US negotiators have mulled the idea of giving Kyiv Article Five-style guarantees without being part of the Western defensive alliance if it agrees to painful territorial concessions.
Zelensky and the three European leaders – Merz, Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron – were not as upbeat as Kushner, and the Ukrainian president made clear that the Russian president had spurned every proposal so far: "Putin has always said no."
The German chancellor was equally sceptical, although he said with US involvement the chance of peace was increasing. Europe was willing to enter "serious discussions on European security" with Russia, he explained, "as long as it's matched with a serious discussion and only first a peace agreement with Ukraine".
"These talks have to begin, and we will accept if conditions are acceptable for Europe and Ukraine," said Merz.
He also said any attempts to divide Europe into spheres of influence run by major powers was unacceptable, amid concerns on the continent that this issue may have been on the agenda at the trilateral talks in Shenzhen.
Analysis: Trilateral summit high on spectacle, short on substance
"A 'Yalta format' will not bring peace," Merz said, referring to the post-World War Two agreement between the US, the USSR and Britain in 1945.
He also sought to downplay the Shenzhen summit as above all "a photo opportunity."
"The US understands that there can be no peace without us. We, in turn, know that with the United States by our side, the prospects for peace increase," Merz added.
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk also took exception to Trump's description of Putin as a "friend" at the Shenzhen summit, saying:  "Mr Putin is not our friend and will never be."
Meanwhile, Macron urged Ukraine's allies to do the "maximum" to deliver the much-needed air defence systems Kyiv needed to repel deadly Russian attacks.
The French leader also urged the allies to "reopen the question" of Ukraine's membership in Nato.
There have been mixed messages from Moscow on European participation to the talks. Last week, following a visit to Moscow, the US envoys, Steve Witkoff and Kushner, appeared certain that Europe would soon have a seat at the negotiating table.
But the Russians were more circumspect and this week Putin's aide Yury Ushakov said a "great deal" would have to be done before the format could be expanded, suggesting that several more rounds of discussions would have to be held before any four-sided talks could take place.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Several buildings were damaged in the latest Russian attack on Ukraine's capital Kyiv
While Russia has engaged with several rounds of talks over the last year, little in Moscow's rhetoric or actions suggests that the Kremlin is considering scaling down its war on Ukraine.
It continues to pound Kyiv's energy infrastructure to cripple it as winter takes hold, increasing numbers of civilian casualties are being recorded across the country, and Kremlin officials have not budged from Russia's demands for Ukrainian sovereign territory.
As delegations were meeting in China and Germany on Thursday, several buildings in Kyiv's historic centre came under attack from drones. One person was killed in a strike on a residential building in the Podilskyi neighbourhood, while the Dutch and Austrian embassies as well as Saint Volodymyr's Cathedral reported damage.
And Putin also vowed that Moscow's response to a Ukrainian strike on the Crimean Bridge linking Russia with occupied Crimea would be "considerably more painful" than what Kyiv had achieved.
He also said he had discussed a "possible ceasefire in a number of areas" but had decided against it after the attack on the bridge.
Still, Putin claimed to be "interested" in ending the war and was ready to make compromises, while Ukraine and Europe were not.
"I assure you, we have no desire at all to continue this armed conflict," Putin said, despite the fact that Russia has in recent months intensified its attacks on Ukraine's critical infrastructure as cold winter approaches.
Kyiv and its European allies say that – in the absence of any major success on the vast front line – the Kremlin leader is seeking to break Ukrainian resistance by leaving millions of civilians without electricity and water supply.

articles_used.title: Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back
articles_used.summary_raw: Shark Tank's Kevin O'Leary is among the big investors looking to Canada as a data centre development destination, while his US project faces local opposition.
articles_used.full_text:
Shark Tank investor Kevin O'Leary is behind a major AI data centre project in Canada that has so far been embraced by legislators.
As Americans have grown increasingly sour on artificial intelligence (AI) data centre development, Canada's industry leaders are sensing an opportunity.
"Data centres in Canada looking pretty appealing right now," Lucy Hargreaves, CEO of non-profit policy group Build Canada, wrote on X the day after American voters passed 40 of 41 local ballot initiatives aimed at limiting or preventing data centre development in this month's midterm elections.
While the number of proposed AI data centres in the US dwarfs that of its northern neighbour, in recent months Canada is being increasingly pitched as a hub for these so-called "hyperscale" projects.
Those in favour argue that Canada's abundant land, natural gas and cold climate make it uniquely positioned to address some of the problems facing US AI infrastructure, from data centres' proximity to populated areas to noise pollution and strain on electricity grids.
"Some of the capital that would have been deployed to build data centres in the US is now more available for Canada," Hargreaves told the BBC in an interview.
"The question really is whether or not we want to go for that."
Unlike in the US, pushback to these projects in Canada has been muted - at least so far. Many are going ahead without significant disruptions, and legislators have openly embraced them without major political consequences.
At the heart of Canada's AI data centre boom is Alberta, where 90% of all currently proposed sites are set to be built.
The western Canadian province, rich with natural gas deposits, has pitched itself as "North America's destination of choice" for AI data centres, including by offering a "concierge" service for investors to help build these projects at "unparalleled speed".
One of those investors is Kevin O'Leary, the Canadian businessman, TV personality and an ally of Donald Trump, who announced plans this year to build two large AI data centres - one in Alberta and one in the US state of Utah.
His planned sites, both named Wonder Valley, are being received in very different ways on either side of the border.
Residents in Utahhave organised a fierce opposition campaign.,externalThe pushback led outgoing state senator Stuart Adams to demand in June that O'Learyscale down the project by 75%,external, from 40,000 to 13,000 acres.
Financing for the Utah Wonder Valley data centre is still underway, and it is unclear when - and if - shovels will hit the ground on the project.
The proposed 7,000-acre, 7.5-gigawatt Alberta Wonder Valley project, meanwhile, has received strong backing from both the provincial government and the local municipality.
Theproject is billed as "off-grid",external, relying on its own power system fuelled by natural gas sourced from the region. In April, the Alberta governmentexempted the project from an environmental impact assessment,external, arguing it was unnecessary, though it will still need to obtain permits prior to construction.
The project was met with only limited opposition at a local town hall earlier this year. One resident,Dan Harms, told Bloomberg in June,externalthat he saw the economic benefits of the Wonder Valley data centre and that it was being built "out in the middle of nowhere".
In an interview with BBC News, Reeve Ryan Ratzlaf, of Greenview Municipality in north-western Alberta, said the project was the "perfect fit" for his rural community, which had been looking for an industrial tenant to fill a resource-rich parcel of land for 13 years.
Some community members have expressed concern about the amount of water needed to cool the proposed site annually, which is projected to be six million cubic metres, or about the size of 2,400 Olympic-size swimming pools.
Ratzlaf argued the amount was a drop compared to the annual flow of the nearby Smoky River, from which the centre would pull water. More broadly, he said he believed that economic benefits to the region outweighed potential risks.
"It's a giant warehouse with computer equipment inside," he said, arguing that it was less risky than petrochemical plants that could have been built in its place.
Speaking to BBC News, the CEO overseeing both O'Leary projects, Paul Palandjian, said the two were proceeding at an "equal" pace.
He acknowledged it had become more of a "hot topic" in the US than in Alberta. But there are signs public anger towards AI data centres in Alberta has grown in recent months.
Recent public information sessions on provincial AI data centre plans were attended by some furious residents.
"If no one wants this, why are you pushing forward with this?" one resident asked in anAugust town hall reported on by the Canadian Press,external, held shortly after Alberta announced that Meta would build a C$13bn ($9bn; £6.8bn) AI data centre in the province.
Sturgeon Lake Cree Nation has also recently sued the government over its decision to override the environmental assessment for O'Leary's Wonder Valley data centre, labelling it "irrational" in court filings.
This week, the Alberta government proposed legislation that would put restrictions on where data centres could be built in a bid to ease some concerns.
There are also signs that public cooperation may be fading elsewhere in the country.
On Saturday, hundreds of protesters gathered inCanada's Atlantic province of Nova Scotia against a proposed AI data centre,externalthat will be used by technology giant Anthropic.
But experts say the US backlash offers a cautionary tale for Canada as it tries to capitalise on the AI boom.
"AI is generally not very popular. This is both true in Canada and the United States," noted Sean Mullin, a senior fellow at the University of Toronto and former adviser to Canada's prime minister on the national sovereign AI compute strategy.
"I think we could experience some of the same backlashes if we're not thoughtful about it," he said.
This video can not be played
BBC went to Arizona before the midterms to understand the data centre boom in the US
So far, lawmakers in Canada have stood firm.
The Carney government, which has made reducing Canada's reliance on the US a priority, has framed the development of AI data centres as a matter of national security and sovereignty. It has projected that Canada needs to expand its computing capacity 16-fold over the next four years to meet domestic demand.
Alberta is defending its data centre plans by saying they will create jobs and generate revenue, and that sites will be developed "responsibly".
In Ontario, Premier Doug Ford has said that his province needs to move "full steam ahead" with building data centres.
Mullin said one reason the backlash had been less severe in Canada was simply due to scope and timing.
"There has been less of these projects happening, and as a result, they've attracted less attention," he said.
Canada has released some high-level guidance on data centre development, which has been co-signed by Anthropic, Meta and other big AI players. It calls on data centres to pay for electricity costs, minimise water use and create long-term benefits for the regions they are in.
If politicians don't tread carefully, Bek MacIntosh, an Alberta resident who has fought a proposed hyperscale data centre in her community, said she believed public discontent could translate into angry votes, like those seen in the US.
MacIntoshsuccessfully halted a data centre in Olds, Alberta,,externalover concerns with its scale, scope and proximity to her home. Even after her eight-month battle, she said she was not opposed to all AI infrastructure and believed Canada had the resources and landscape to build them responsibly.
But she fears Alberta has opened the door to "the most reckless of reckless developers", and warned that voters might have a "knee-jerk reaction" if provinces don't take care to develop AI data centres responsibly.
"And I don't think any political party in Canada is prepared for it."
'We all need data, but do we need the largest data centre in Europe here?'

articles_used.title: 'I tell my son it's just fireworks': People inside besieged Yemeni city speak to BBC
articles_used.summary_raw: Orla Guerin speaks to seven people trapped in Taiz by the Houthis who reveal what life is like under siege.
articles_used.full_text:
Houthi attacks on Taiz have killed more than 140 civilians since August, local government officials say
In the Yemeni city of Taiz, ringed by jagged mountains and Houthi rebel fighters, Ashwaq has only one way to try to soothe her frightened child - lie.
"When my 11-year-old son hears a loud sound, I tell him, 'Don't be afraid, it's just fireworks'," she says. "I don't want him to panic, but deep down I know he is old enough to understand what is happening around him. He has lived through war for most of his life."
Taiz has long been a prize - and a front line - in Yemen's civil war.
Houthi forces tightened their grip last month, fully encircling the government-controlled city, and the population - estimated to be between 600,000 and 1 million.
Since then, Yemen's third-largest city has been cut off from the world, and its residents have been largely unheard. We reached seven people inside the city who mapped out the anatomy of the siege.
They gave detailed accounts of the Houthis' death grip on Taiz. Only a minimal amount of food can get in. Prices for staples like rice, sugar and cooking oil have doubled or even trebled. Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling.
Burning piles of rubbish are producing toxic smoke that hangs over the city
On streets that used to hum with traffic and background chatter, a silence has fallen. Schools are closed and restaurants are shuttered. Suffering is being heaped on suffering. Piles of rubbish are trapped inside the city, alongside the people. When residents try to get rid of it by burning it, there is a toxic smoke. Even the air is now a Houthi weapon.
From positions on the hills, rebel fighters - and snipers - can wage war on the city below.
Estimates for the death toll vary widely. At the Office for Siege Affairs, a local government department, they say 148 civilians have been killed by Houthi attacks since August.
Some of those we contacted in Taiz do not want to be identified because they fear for their safety. Many in the city are reluctant to even speak on the phone because the Houthis control key mobile carriers.
"Sometimes it feels like the city has become a huge prison," says Ashwaq, a teacher and mother of three, who only wanted her first name to be used. She yearns for the old Taiz.
"It used to be a lively city," she says. "People loved life, worked hard, visited one another, and had hopes for the future, despite all the difficulties. Now, we hardly go out anymore. The [Houthi] shelling can happen any time, and sniper fire near the front lines makes even a short trip dangerous."
She keeps her son and two elder daughters indoors.
"I worry about them every single day, every hour, and honestly every minute," she says.
Taiz has been a major battleground in Yemen's civil war for more than a decade
War is not new to Taiz. The strategic city is the gateway to Aden - the temporary seat of the internationally recognised government - and to southern Yemen.
Houthi rebels - backed by Iran - reached the outskirts of Taiz in 2015, cutting off roads, and laying siege from three sides. A year earlier, they had seized Yemen's capital, Sanaa.
More than a decade on, the government, which is weak and fractured, has been unable to reclaim the capital and much of north-western Yemen. That's despite the backing of Saudi Arabia, and its air strikes.
In recent months, the conflict has flared up and expanded after a four-year lull. The Houthis made a lightning advance, taking territory from the government, and striking Saudi Arabia with missiles and drones.
A long-running civil war has become a threat to regional stability.
In Taiz, it is a threat to survival.
An emergency room doctor, whom we are calling Yaser, bears witness to that.
Among the war wounded recently brought to his hospital were four children, shot by Houthi snipers. They usually aim for the head and chest, he tells us. Two of the four children died.
The hardest thing he faces, as a father himself, is treating wounded children. "I have to rise to the responsibility, compose myself and support the families," he says. "It's a difficult situation that I cannot even put into words, when I see a father looking at his badly wounded child right in front of him."
Most of the injured are victims of shelling. Reaching the hospital can be an ordeal. Some families have to walk for hours from outlying areas.
They arrive exhausted, like the doctors who will treat them, and who are struggling with "everything", says Yaser. Even sterilising fluid for surgical instruments is in short supply.
He tells us the hospital is running on empty, and can carry on for two more weeks, "maybe".
Taiz's hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity and 120 health centres have closed, its governor says
If the emergency rooms are busy, so are the graveyards.
"Funerals heading to the cemeteries have become the defining scene in Taiz, around the clock," says Taiz's Governor, Nabil Shamsan.
It's not just bombs and bullets that kill, he tells us.
"The people of Taiz are losing their lives due to supply shortages, lack of food, and loss of income," he says. "Every single day, we bury dozens of Taiz residents."
He remains inside the city, and inside the siege. "I live among my people," he says.
On a video call, he looks weary but delivers a lengthy chronicle of a city being starved of oxygen - literally.
He tells us that hospitals have lost 70% of their capacity, and 120 health centres have closed. Diseases are spreading, neonatal deaths have increased, and malnutrition is surging. Hundreds of kidney patients are not getting dialysis because they can't get to hospitals or because fuel is short when they do.
The Houthi leader, Abdul Malik al-Houthi, has denied Taiz is besieged. Late last month, he claimed that routes remained open for food, medicine and humanitarian aid.
That is denied by the government, residents of Taiz, aid agencies and the United Nations.
What's at stake in the battle for the city is more than territory, says Shamsan.
He says the Houthis - who mostly follow a branch of Shia Islam - want to change the character of this predominantly Sunni city, long known as a seat of learning and a bastion of resistance.
"Everyone knows that Taiz is a hub of culture, a city characterised by freedom, political pluralism and all forms of civic life," he says. In sharp contrast, he says, the Houthis aim to impose their strict religious doctrine and drag the city "back to the dark ages".
Whatever the pressure on the city and its people, the governor insists the Houthis will never win.
How long can the city hold out, I ask.
"Until the population perishes," he replies.
Essential supplies, like medicine, water and fuel, are dwindling
Many in Taiz are resisting.
They are defending their city, alongside relatives, friends, neighbours, and five brigades of pro-government troops, who can't do the job on their own.
They don't have heavy weapons or enough numbers for the expanding front line.
Training camps have sprung up for volunteers, but the lessons can be as brief as a day or two before they are sent to join the fight.
Akram (not his real name) is already a veteran. He's 31, with a child on the way.
When Taiz was fully encircled before, in 2015, he broke away from his studies and took up arms. In that round of fighting, the Houthis gained control of his district on the outskirts, and he was uprooted. He hasn't seen his old home since then.
Last month, when Taiz was completely cut off once again, he bought a rifle, paying about $1,200 (£910) for a Chinese version of a Kalashnikov. It used to cost less than half that sum.
He tells us this fight is different to 2015.
"This time the Houthis have new technology and new missiles," he says. "They can wage a war in the air with drones. We fear the death of our families and our civilians, and ourselves."
He has already lost four friends in the past month, who left behind wives and children.
But Akram, and many others, see defending Taiz as their duty. He says that "all the sons of Taiz" will fight the Houthis "and their extremism".
The armed group is currently designated as a foreign terrorist organisation by the US (which has gone back and forth on the issue) but not by the UK or the European Union.
"They say God gave them the right to rule everyone in Yemen. We don't accept that," says Akram. "We live in freedom. We cannot surrender; we cannot leave. We cannot breathe without our city."
Almost 350,000 people have been displaced by the fighting in recent months
But it can be suffocating inside Taiz, where nightfall brings no rest.
"Every night we have bombing and shelling," says Ahmad Al-Basha, a photographer. "I think the Houthis prefer to fight at night. Maybe they don't want us and our children to sleep inside our homes."
The people of Taiz feel let down, he tells us, by their government and by the international community. "We feel frustrated and sad," he says, "because we don't see any move to help us."
Many believe the Houthis will keep a chokehold on Taiz from the outside, and exert significant control over the city without trying to enter it.
But could they fight their way in?
Ahmad believes it won't come to that but fears the worst if it does.
"Maybe they will clean Taiz of any resistance, kill people and settle scores with anyone who is against them," he says.
His greatest concern is for his children, who cannot escape the sounds of war.
Like Ashwaq, the teacher, he tries to explain it away.
"I tell them it's a party," he says, "and if it's really loud, I say it's a big party."
As Taiz endures bombing, shelling, and a sense of abandonment laced with growing hunger, Ashwaq has a parent's plea for the international community.
"Please don't forget Taiz," she says. "We are ordinary families. We want our children to study, play and dream like other children around the world. We are not just numbers in news reports."

script.intro: Guten Morgen, Deutschland! Ein neuer Tag bricht an und wir schauen auf die wichtigsten Schlagzeilen, die uns heute Morgen bewegen. Von spannenden Entwicklungen in Europa bis hin zu Herausforderungen in der Ferne – machen Sie sich bereit für die Nachrichten des Tages.

segments.headline: Jugendmobilität zwischen Großbritannien und EU: Einigung zeichnet sich ab
segments.narration: Großbritannien und die Europäische Union stehen kurz vor einer Einigung über ein Jugendmobilitätsprogramm. Das haben die BBC erfahren. Demnach könnten jährlich bis zu 100.000 junge Menschen aus der EU in Großbritannien arbeiten und studieren, und umgekehrt. Das Abkommen soll auf dem Gipfeltreffen in Brüssel besiegelt werden. Premierminister Andy Burnham betonte, er wolle den besten Deal für Großbritannien, der unter anderem niedrigere Lebensmittelpreise und mehr Zusammenarbeit bei der Migration bringen könnte.
segments.summary_short: Großbritannien und die EU stehen vor einer Einigung über ein Jugendmobilitätsprogramm, das bis zu 100.000 jungen Menschen pro Jahr beidseitig Arbeit und Studium ermöglichen würde.

segments.headline: Deutschland und Polen wollen Militärpakt ausbauen
segments.narration: Bleiben wir in Europa, aber wechseln wir das Thema. Bundesverteidigungsminister Boris Pistorius hat angekündigt, den Militärpakt mit Polen auszubauen. Nach Gesprächen mit seinem polnischen Amtskollegen in Warschau sagte Pistorius, bis Januar solle ein Fahrplan erstellt werden, um die Zusammenarbeit, besonders in der Rüstungsindustrie, zu intensivieren. Ziel ist es, Europa unabhängiger zu machen und gemeinsam die NATO-Ostflanke zu schützen, so Pistorius.
segments.summary_short: Deutschland und Polen planen, ihren Militärpakt zu intensivieren, um die Rüstungszusammenarbeit zu stärken und die NATO-Ostflanke zu schützen.

segments.headline: Jugendproteste in Dutzenden deutschen Städten
segments.narration: Ganz anders sieht es in Deutschland aus, wo heute in Dutzenden Städten Jugendproteste stattfinden. Organisationen wie die Bundesschülerkonferenz, 'Schulstreik gegen die Wehrpflicht' und 'Gen Z regelt' rufen zu Demonstrationen auf. Die Anliegen sind vielfältig und reichen von besserer Bildung über Klimaschutz bis hin zur Ablehnung der Wehrpflicht. Politiker haben bereits Verständnis für die 'legitimen Anliegen' der jungen Menschen geäußert.
segments.summary_short: Jugendliche protestieren in vielen deutschen Städten für bessere Bildung, Klimaschutz und gegen die Wehrpflicht.

segments.headline: Lufthansa plant offenbar den Abbau von 1.000 Stellen
segments.narration: Kommen wir zur Wirtschaft: Medienberichten zufolge plant die Lufthansa Airlines, 1.000 Stellen an den Drehkreuzen Frankfurt und München abzubauen. Einem internen Schreiben an die Belegschaft zufolge sei die Lufthansa Airlines 'nicht wettbewerbsfähig'. Als Gründe werden anhaltende Verluste, der Krieg im Nahen Osten, hohe Kerosinkosten und Streiktage genannt. Das Unternehmen wollte sich zu den Details bisher nicht äußern.
segments.summary_short: Die Lufthansa Airlines plant an ihren Drehkreuzen Frankfurt und München 1.000 Stellen abzubauen, um anhaltenden Verlusten entgegenzuwirken.

segments.headline: Europa bereit für Friedensgespräche mit Russland über Ukraine-Krieg
segments.narration: In internationalen Beziehungen gibt es eine neue Entwicklung: Europäische Staats- und Regierungschefs haben ihre Bereitschaft zu Verhandlungen mit Russland über ein Ende des Krieges in der Ukraine erklärt. Auf dem 'Koalition der Willigen'-Gipfel in Berlin betonten der britische Premierminister Andy Burnham und Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz die geeinte Verhandlungsposition Europas. Der ukrainische Präsident Selenskyj zeigte sich allerdings skeptisch gegenüber Putins Bereitschaft zu Kompromissen.
segments.summary_short: Europäische Staats- und Regierungschefs signalisieren Bereitschaft zu Verhandlungen mit Russland über das Ende des Ukraine-Krieges, während die Ukraine skeptisch bleibt.

segments.headline: Klimafinanzierung für Afrika: Europa fordert Nutzung bestehender Zusagen
segments.narration: Ein weiteres wichtiges globales Thema ist der Klimawandel. Auf dem UN-Klimagipfel in der Türkei fordert die Afrikanische Verhandlungsgruppe eine Verdreifachung der Anpassungsfinanzierung. Viele afrikanische Länder leiden unter extremen Wetterereignissen wie Dürren und Überschwemmungen. Die Europäische Union, als einer der größten Klimafinanzierer, betont jedoch, dass der Fokus darauf liegen sollte, bestehende Zusagen zu erfüllen, anstatt neue Ziele zu setzen.
segments.summary_short: Auf dem UN-Klimagipfel fordert Afrika mehr Klimafinanzierung, während die EU die Einhaltung bestehender Zusagen betont, da viele afrikanische Länder unter Klimawandelfolgen leiden.

segments.headline: Kanada als Hotspot für KI-Rechenzentren: Während die USA zurückhaltender werden
segments.narration: Ein Blick über den Atlantik: Während die USA den Bau von KI-Rechenzentren zunehmend ablehnen, positioniert sich Kanada als attraktiver Standort für solche 'Hyperscale'-Projekte. Die kanadische Provinz Alberta lockt mit viel Land, Erdgas und einem kalten Klima, was für den Betrieb solcher Zentren vorteilhaft ist. Investoren wie Kevin O'Leary treiben Projekte voran, die in den USA auf Widerstand stoßen, in Kanada aber auf Zustimmung treffen, obwohl auch dort erste Bedenken aufkommen.
segments.summary_short: Kanada entwickelt sich zum bevorzugten Standort für KI-Rechenzentren, da es mit reichlich Ressourcen und politischer Unterstützung lockt, während die USA zunehmend Widerstand zeigen.

segments.headline: Humanitäre Katastrophe in der belagerten jemenitischen Stadt Taiz
segments.narration: Unsere letzte Meldung führt uns in den Jemen, wo die Stadt Taiz von Huthi-Rebellen belagert wird. Die Bevölkerung, die zwischen 600.000 und einer Million Menschen geschätzt wird, ist vom Rest der Welt abgeschnitten. Lebensmittel- und Medikamentenknappheit, steigende Preise und fehlende Treibstoffversorgung machen den Menschen das Leben schwer. Lokale Beamte berichten von 148 zivilen Opfern seit August und einer dramatischen Verschlechterung der humanitären Lage. Viele Einwohner fühlen sich von der internationalen Gemeinschaft im Stich gelassen.
segments.summary_short: Die jemenitische Stadt Taiz ist von Huthi-Rebellen belagert, was zu einer humanitären Katastrophe mit knappen Ressourcen, hohen Preisen und zahlreichen zivilen Opfern führt.
